summary:
Anambra is a state in south-eastern Nigeria, capital Awka, formed in 1976 and Igbo-majority in population. It sits outside the twelve northern Nigerian states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty provisions those states provide for male sodomy do not reach Anambra; the federal statutory penalties apply here in full.

Same-sex sexual activity in Anambra carries the secular statutory maximum of up to 14 years' imprisonment under Nigeria's national framework, which governs the state. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act extends criminalisation to attempted same-sex marriages.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country, including Anambra.

LGBTQ+ people in Anambra have no legal protections under Nigerian law and face violence; the national record documents police torture, arbitrary arrests, mass arrests at private gatherings and hotels, and unprosecuted killings of transgender women.
tangentialFactors:
Anambra's position in the south-east places it outside the northern Shari'a zone, so the death-penalty exposure reported for the twelve northern states does not apply here; the operative exposure is the secular statutory maximum of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The national record documents 'kito' gangs using dating applications to lure, beat, film and blackmail LGBTQ+ Nigerians, a pattern that reaches users in any state including Anambra, with the threat of disclosure as the leverage.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported in September 2022 were met with fear among transgender Nigerians; the national record does not document whether such a proposal has been enacted in Anambra.
localsOnly:
Residents of Anambra live under Nigeria's national framework: same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and LGBTQ+ people have no legal protections. The 2022 court ruling striking Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act applies nationwide, including in Anambra.

The national record documents that many LGBTQ+ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to the police because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk; this fear is documented nationally and is not sourced to Anambra specifically.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Anambra-specific incidents of violence, arrests, or police practice; all enforcement evidence in the parent framework is drawn from other Nigerian states (Lagos, Delta, Gombe, Bauchi) and is not attributed to Anambra.

Whether the 2022 constitutional ruling has been applied in Anambra courts, or how Anambra police enforce the remaining provisions, is not sourced in this inventory.

The current status of the reported cross-dressing criminalisation proposals, and whether Anambra's state legislature has acted on them, is unresolved in the available sources.
